scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated in African American communities across the rural South, with early roots in New Orleans during the first decade of the 20th century and connections to Nashville and Atlanta.
Perry Bradford and Gus Horsley copyrighted the 'Original Black Bottom Dance' in August 1926.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: With its prominent pelvic shifts and uninhibited energy, the Black Bottom was considered provocative and daring by society at large.
It transitioned from marginalized southern communities and tent shows into a celebrated mainstream performance and social craze.
Today it is a historical tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Black Bottom (https://archive.org/details/the-real-black-bottom-dance-1927)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The Black Bottom was danced solo or by couples to syncopated 4/4 jazz rhythms.

Basic steps included hopping down front, sliding or 'doodling' back, mooching left and right by leading with the hips, placing hands on hips to do the 'mess around', and performing a hobbling 'break a leg' step near the ground.
It was also characterized by strong pelvic movements and playful rear bumps.
Watch for The Mooch, Break a Leg.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (rQ9qapVmWi4)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Danced solo or by couples in ballrooms, cabarets, and stages

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance was performed to upbeat jazz music in a syncopated 4/4 meter.

Key musical works associated with the dance include Jelly Roll Morton's 'Black Bottom Stomp' and the hit song 'Black Bottom' composed by Ray Henderson, Buddy DeSylva, and Lew Brown, which received numerous commercial recordings in 1926.
Listen for the piano.
The pulse is 4/4.
Syncopated 4/4 jazz music featuring prominent piano, driving rhythm, and playful stomp tempos reminiscent of 1920s revues.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The dance was performed in cabarets, tent shows, Broadway revues, and mainstream ballrooms.
Costuming reflected the vibrant 1920s Jazz Age fashion, famously associated with flappers and tuxedoed dancers.
on_screen: Image gallery: 2 licensed images with attribution

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include Ann Pennington and Tom Patricola who popularized it on Broadway, African American dancer and choreographer Billy Pierce who introduced it, collaborator Buddy Bradley, and composers Jelly Roll Morton and Perry Bradford.
The dance took on many variations across semirural southern tent shows and urban centers like New Orleans, Atlanta, Nashville, and Detroit before being standardized for Broadway stages.

Rooted in African American traditional dance of the early 20th century, the Black Bottom developed alongside and eventually rivaled the Charleston, later influencing mid-century cinematic choreography and stage revivals.
